subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, and head and neck cancer
vignette: A 34-year-old woman has 10 days of facial pain and pressure over her right cheek, worse when bending forward, with nasal congestion and purulent discharge. CT shows opacification of the right maxillary sinus with an obstructed outflow tract.
question: Which sinus is most likely affected, and what best explains its predisposition to impaired drainage?

options.text: Frontal sinus; its ostium opens at the floor and drains freely with gravity
Sphenoid sinus; its ostium is located inferolaterally and drains against gravity
Maxillary sinus; its ostium is superomedial, so drainage occurs against gravity
Anterior ethmoid sinus; its ostium lies in the superior meatus
Posterior ethmoid sinus; it drains into the inferior meatus

explanation_correct: Obstruction of sinus drainage into the nasal cavity produces inflammation and pain over the affected area. The maxillary sinus is typically affected because its ostium is located superomedially, so it must drain against gravity. This patient's cheek pain and CT opacification localize to the maxillary sinus.

explanation_incorrect.A: The frontal sinus drains via the frontonasal duct into the middle meatus; its drainage is not described as against gravity, and forehead rather than cheek pain would be expected.
explanation_incorrect.B: The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess, not through a superomedial ostium that drains against gravity, and it is not the classic sinus affected in this way.
explanation_incorrect.D: Anterior ethmoid air cells drain into the middle meatus and their ostia are not superomedial; cheek pain points instead to the maxillary sinus.
explanation_incorrect.E: Posterior ethmoid air cells drain into the superior meatus, not the inferior meatus; the inferior meatus drains the nasolacrimal duct.

educationalObjective: The maxillary sinus is the sinus most often affected by rhinosinusitis because its superomedial ostium forces drainage against gravity.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, and head and neck cancer
vignette: A 28-year-old man with persistent sinusitis undergoes nasal endoscopy. The otolaryngologist notes that a single meatus receives drainage from the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses, while a different meatus serves as the outlet for the nasolacrimal duct.
question: Which of the following correctly pairs a nasal meatus with the structure that drains into it?

options.text: Middle meatus - frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses
Superior meatus - frontal and maxillary sinuses
Inferior meatus - posterior ethmoid air cells
Superior meatus - nasolacrimal duct
Middle meatus - sphenoid sinus

explanation_correct: The middle meatus drains the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses. The superior meatus drains the posterior ethmoid air cells, the inferior meatus drains the nasolacrimal duct, and the sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess.

explanation_incorrect.B: The superior meatus drains the posterior ethmoid air cells; the frontal and maxillary sinuses drain into the middle meatus.
explanation_incorrect.C: The inferior meatus drains the nasolacrimal duct; posterior ethmoid air cells drain into the superior meatus.
explanation_incorrect.D: The nasolacrimal duct drains into the inferior meatus, not the superior meatus.
explanation_incorrect.E: The sphenoid sinus drains into the sphenoethmoidal recess; the middle meatus drains the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses.

educationalObjective: The middle meatus drains the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses; the inferior meatus drains the nasolacrimal duct and the superior meatus drains the posterior ethmoid.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, and head and neck cancer
vignette: A 24-year-old college student develops nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, sneezing, and facial pressure following an upper respiratory infection. Symptoms are worst during the first week and begin to improve by day 10 without antibiotics.
question: Which pathogen is most likely responsible for this episode of acute rhinosinusitis?

options.text: Nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae
Rhinovirus
Streptococcus pneumoniae
Moraxella catarrhalis
Epstein-Barr virus

explanation_correct: Acute rhinosinusitis is most commonly caused by viruses, with rhinovirus a classic example. The illness is usually self-limited, improving within about 10 days. Bacterial infection may superimpose on a viral infection, but it is not the usual cause of uncomplicated acute sinusitis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Nontypeable H influenzae is a common cause of bacterial rhinosinusitis that may superimpose on a viral infection, not the usual cause of uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: S pneumoniae is a bacterial pathogen that may cause superimposed bacterial sinusitis, typically with symptoms persisting beyond 10 days or severe fever and purulent discharge.
explanation_incorrect.D: M catarrhalis is another bacterium associated with secondary bacterial sinusitis, not the most common cause of acute rhinosinusitis.
explanation_incorrect.E: EBV causes infectious mononucleosis and is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not acute rhinosinusitis.

educationalObjective: Acute rhinosinusitis is usually viral (eg, rhinovirus); bacterial superimposition is most often due to nontypeable H influenzae, S pneumoniae, or M catarrhalis.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, and head and neck cancer
vignette: A 19-year-old has 2 weeks of worsening right facial pain, fever, and purulent nasal discharge. He then develops right periorbital swelling, proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and decreased vision. Imaging shows inflammation extending from the paranasal sinuses into the orbital apex and cavernous sinus.
question: Which complication best explains these new findings?

options.text: Otitis media with effusion from eustachian tube obstruction
Laryngeal papillomatosis with upper airway obstruction
Subcutaneous emphysema with a positive Hamman sign
Orbital cellulitis with cavernous sinus syndrome from sinus infection extension
Fibrosing mediastinitis due to Histoplasma infection

explanation_correct: Paranasal sinus infections may extend to the orbits, cavernous sinus, and brain, causing complications such as orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus syndrome, and meningitis. Periorbital swelling, proptosis, and ophthalmoplegia in the setting of sinusitis indicate orbital involvement with extension toward the cavernous sinus.

explanation_incorrect.A: Eustachian tube obstruction with otitis media and effusion is seen with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not with direct extension of sinus infection into the orbit.
explanation_incorrect.B: Laryngeal papillomatosis is a benign HPV-6/11 tumor of the vocal cords causing hoarseness, not an orbital complication of sinusitis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Subcutaneous emphysema and Hamman sign are features of pneumomediastinum, not sinusitis extending to the orbit.
explanation_incorrect.E: Fibrosing mediastinitis is a chronic connective tissue proliferation in the mediastinum associated with Histoplasma, unrelated to sinus infection.

educationalObjective: Untreated paranasal sinusitis can extend into the orbit, cavernous sinus, and brain, producing orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus syndrome, or meningitis.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, and head and neck cancer
vignette: A 16-year-old boy has recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds from the anterior part of his nose and a vascular mass in the nasopharynx. A separate 68-year-old man has a severe posterior nosebleed requiring packing and cautery to control bleeding.
question: Which statement best distinguishes the vascular source of bleeding in these two patients?

options.text: Both bleeds arise from Kiesselbach plexus located in the posterior septum
The adolescent's bleed is from the sphenopalatine artery and the elderly man's is from Kiesselbach plexus
The sphenopalatine artery is a branch of the facial artery
Kiesselbach plexus is in the posterior septum and is the most common site of life-threatening hemorrhage
The anterior bleed is from Kiesselbach plexus on the caudal septum; life-threatening posterior bleeds are from the sphenopalatine artery, a maxillary artery branch

explanation_correct: Epistaxis most commonly occurs in the anterior segment of the nostril at Kiesselbach plexus on the caudal septum, supplied by the superior labial, anterior and posterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, and sphenopalatine arteries. Life-threatening posterior hemorrhage arises from the sphenopalatine artery, a branch of the maxillary artery. Nasal angiofibromas are a cause of epistaxis in adolescent males.

explanation_incorrect.A: Kiesselbach plexus is in the anterior (caudal) septum, not posterior, and the severe posterior bleed here is from the sphenopalatine artery.
explanation_incorrect.B: The relationships are reversed: the common anterior bleed is from Kiesselbach plexus and the life-threatening posterior bleed is from the sphenopalatine artery.
explanation_incorrect.C: The sphenopalatine artery is a branch of the maxillary artery, not the facial artery.
explanation_incorrect.D: Kiesselbach plexus is anterior and causes common, usually not life-threatening bleeds; life-threatening posterior hemorrhage is from the sphenopalatine artery.

educationalObjective: Anterior epistaxis usually originates from Kiesselbach plexus on the caudal septum, while life-threatening posterior epistaxis originates from the sphenopalatine artery, a maxillary artery branch.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, and head and neck cancer
vignette: A 58-year-old man with a long history of tobacco and alcohol use develops unilateral nasal obstruction, bloody nasal discharge, and recurrent epistaxis. He also has a persistent unilateral middle ear effusion and hearing loss. Biopsy reveals a malignant nasopharyngeal tumor.
question: Which etiologic association and mechanism best explain this tumor and the ear findings?

options.text: HPV-16 infection causing oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with field cancerization
EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma; tumor-related eustachian tube obstruction causes the middle ear effusion and hearing loss
HPV-6/11 infection causing benign laryngeal papillomatosis of the true vocal cords
Tobacco- and alcohol-related laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma causing supraglottic dysphagia
EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma that directly invades the middle ear to cause otitis media

explanation_correct: Head and neck cancers are mostly squamous cell carcinoma, with risk factors including tobacco, alcohol, HPV-16 for oropharyngeal tumors, and EBV for nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma presents with unilateral nasal obstruction, discharge, and epistaxis, and eustachian tube obstruction can lead to otitis media with effusion and hearing loss.

explanation_incorrect.A: HPV-16 is linked to oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma with field cancerization, but unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and eustachian tube obstruction localize to the nasopharynx, which is associated with EBV.
explanation_incorrect.C: HPV-6/11 causes benign laryngeal papillomatosis (recurrent respiratory papillomatosis) of the true vocal cords with hoarseness, not nasopharyngeal carcinoma with epistaxis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Tobacco and alcohol are risk factors for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, but the unilateral nasal obstruction, epistaxis, and middle ear effusion point to EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
explanation_incorrect.E: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma produces middle ear effusion by obstructing the eustachian tube, not by directly invading the middle ear; the effusion is secondary to obstruction.

educationalObjective: EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma causes unilateral nasal obstruction and epistaxis, and may produce otitis media with effusion and hearing loss through eustachian tube obstruction.

subject: Respiratory
subtopic: Rhinosinusitis, epistaxis, and head and neck cancer
vignette: A 3-year-old boy has had progressive hoarseness and a weak cry since birth. Endoscopy shows multiple small, wart-like benign masses on the true vocal cords. His mother had genital warts during pregnancy. A 55-year-old man with similar masses has difficulty swallowing rather than hoarseness.
question: Which viral type and lesion location best explain these findings?

options.text: HPV-16; oropharyngeal palatine tonsil
EBV; nasopharynx
HPV-6/11; supraglottic region causing hoarseness
HPV-6/11; true vocal cords, with supraglottic lesions causing dysphagia
HPV-6/11; infraglottic region causing dysphagia

explanation_correct: Laryngeal papillomatosis (recurrent respiratory papillomatosis) is a benign tumor associated with HPV-6 and HPV-11, often affecting stratified squamous epithelium such as the true vocal cords and especially children, possibly from vertical transmission during labor. Symptoms localize disease: supraglottic lesions cause dysphagia, while glottic or infraglottic lesions cause hoarseness.

explanation_incorrect.A: HPV-16 is associated with oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, not benign recurrent respiratory papillomatosis of the vocal cords.
explanation_incorrect.B: EBV is associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not benign laryngeal papillomas of the vocal cords.
explanation_incorrect.C: HPV-6/11 is correct, but supraglottic lesions cause dysphagia, not hoarseness; hoarseness localizes to glottic or infraglottic disease.
explanation_incorrect.E: HPV-6/11 is correct, but infraglottic or glottic lesions cause hoarseness, whereas dysphagia indicates supraglottic disease.

educationalObjective: Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is a benign HPV-6/11 tumor of the true vocal cords in children; supraglottic lesions cause dysphagia while glottic/infraglottic lesions cause hoarseness.
